# Intro

<!-- scene: in_s01 -->
Hold an object up to a lamp, and it throws a shadow on the wall. [pause 0.6s] Turn it a little, and the shadow changes. [pause 1.0s] From most sides, this one looks like a shapeless blob. [pause 0.8s] But from one direction, three separate groups appear, with a spiral running through them. [pause 1.2s] A shadow is flat. [pause 0.3s] It always throws a dimension away. [pause 0.5s] The question is which view throws away the least.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: in_s02 -->
Data has the same problem, only worse. [pause 0.4s] Take a scan of a handwritten digit. [pause 0.3s] It's a small grid of sixty-four squares, each one some shade of gray. [pause 0.6s] Write those shades down in a row, and one digit becomes sixty-four numbers. [pause 0.8s] Two numbers, we can plot on a page. [pause 0.3s] Three, we can turn in our hands. [pause 0.6s] Sixty-four, nobody can picture. [pause 0.8s] And this table has almost eighteen hundred rows.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: in_s03 -->
So let's ask the data for its best shadow. [pause 0.5s] Squeeze every digit down from sixty-four numbers to just two, and plot each one as a dot. [pause 1.5s] Nobody told the method which digit is which. [pause 0.6s] And still the zeros gather in one place, the sixes in another, the fours somewhere else. [pause 1.0s] Two numbers out of sixty-four, and much of the structure survives. [pause 0.6s] The method that found this view is called principal component analysis, or *PCA*.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: in_s04 -->
It shows up all over science. [pause 0.4s] Feed it the genes of people across Europe, and its best shadow looks a lot like a map of Europe. [pause 0.8s] Feed it photos of faces, and it finds a small set of ghostly base faces that every face is built from. [pause 0.8s] It shrinks images and cleans up noisy signals. [pause 0.4s] And in finance, it finds that interest rates mostly move in just three ways: they rise together, they tilt, or they bend. [pause 1.2s] Whenever there are too many measurements to look at, PCA is one of the first tools people reach for.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: in_s05 -->
The idea is older than computers. [pause 0.4s] In nineteen oh one, Karl Pearson looked for the line that passes closest to a cloud of points. [pause 0.5s] In nineteen thirty three, Harold Hotelling looked for the directions in which data varies the most, and he named them principal components. [pause 0.8s] They turned out to be the same answer. [pause 1.0s] We'll build it one step at a time: data as a cloud of points, the best direction, one matrix, its eigenvectors, cutting the dimensions down, and where it all breaks. [pause 1.0s] By the end, that map of digits will make complete sense.

> [pause 2]

# Data as a Cloud

<!-- scene: ch1_s01 -->
Let's start small. [pause 0.3s] Forty people, and two measurements each: height, and arm span, the distance from fingertip to fingertip with arms stretched out. [pause 0.8s] Each row of the table is one person. [pause 0.3s] Give each person a dot, with height along one axis and arm span along the other. [pause 1.2s] The dots don't scatter at random. [pause 0.4s] They lean along a diagonal, because taller people tend to have longer arms. [pause 0.6s] Leonardo da Vinci noticed this more than five hundred years ago: for most people, arm span is close to height.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch1_s02 -->
The first step is to find the centre of the cloud. [pause 0.4s] Average all the heights, average all the arm spans, and you get one point: the average person. [pause 0.8s] Then slide the whole cloud so the average person sits at zero. [pause 1.0s] Nothing about the shape changes. [pause 0.3s] We only stop caring where the cloud is, so we can study how it's spread out.

> [pause 1]

<!-- scene: ch1_s03 -->
How spread out is it? [pause 0.4s] Take each person's height, see how far it is from the average height, square that gap, and average the squares. [pause 0.6s] That number is the variance. [pause 0.8s] Squaring makes every gap count as positive, and it makes far points count much more than near ones. [pause 1.0s] We can measure the spread along height, and along arm span. [pause 0.5s] But look along the diagonal. [pause 0.4s] The cloud stretches further that way than along either one. [pause 0.8s] The directions we happened to measure in are not the directions the data cares about.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch1_s04 -->
Add a third measurement, say shoulder width, and every person becomes a point in three dimensions. [pause 1.0s] The cloud is still there. [pause 0.3s] We just need to turn it to see its shape. [pause 0.8s] The digits work the same way. [pause 0.4s] Sixty-four shades in a column make one point in a space with sixty-four directions. [pause 0.8s] We can't turn that cloud to look at it. [pause 0.5s] So we need a way to find its best view by calculation instead.

> [pause 2]

# The Best Direction

<!-- scene: ch2_s01 -->
Back to two dimensions, where we can see everything. [pause 0.4s] Draw a line through the centre, and drop every point straight onto it, at a right angle. [pause 0.6s] Those landing spots are the shadows of the points on this line. [pause 1.0s] Now turn the line. [pause 0.5s] Pointing one way, the shadows bunch up together. [pause 0.4s] Pointing another, they spread far apart. [pause 1.0s] Let's record the spread of the shadows for every angle. [pause 1.5s] The record has one clear peak. [pause 0.4s] That direction keeps the most spread, and it's the first principal component.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch2_s02 -->
There's a second way to pick a best line. [pause 0.4s] Pearson wanted the line that passes closest to the points, with the smallest total of squared gaps. [pause 0.8s] Look at one point. [pause 0.3s] Its distance from the centre is fixed. [pause 0.4s] Its shadow and its gap to the line make a right triangle, with that distance as the long side. [pause 0.8s] By Pythagoras, the shadow squared and the gap squared always add up to the same thing. [pause 1.0s] So when the shadows grow, the gaps must shrink. [pause 0.6s] The line with the most spread is the line that fits closest. [pause 0.4s] Pearson's line and Hotelling's direction are the same.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch2_s03 -->
To compute this, describe the direction with an arrow one unit long. [pause 0.5s] A point's shadow on that line is the dot product of the point with the arrow. [pause 0.8s] Square each shadow and average over all the points, and you get the variance in that direction. [pause 1.0s] So the whole problem fits in one sentence. [pause 0.4s] Among all arrows of length one, find the one that makes this average as big as possible.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: ch2_s04 -->
One direction rarely tells the whole story. [pause 0.4s] Look for the best direction again, but only among those at a right angle to the first. [pause 0.6s] That's the second principal component. [pause 0.3s] It picks up the spread the first one missed. [pause 1.0s] Turn the grid to line up with these two, and every person gets new coordinates. [pause 0.6s] Along the first axis, people differ in overall size. [pause 0.4s] Along the second, in whether their arms are long or short for their height. [pause 1.0s] Same people, same cloud, but the axes finally mean something.

> [pause 2]

# The Covariance Matrix

<!-- scene: ch3_s01 -->
Searching every angle works in two dimensions. [pause 0.4s] In sixty-four, there are far too many directions to try. [pause 0.6s] We need the answer directly. [pause 0.8s] Start from the formula for the variance along an arrow. [pause 0.4s] Write each shadow as a small matrix product, and regroup. [pause 0.8s] The arrow moves to the outside, and everything about the data collects in the middle. [pause 1.0s] That middle part is a single matrix, built once from the data. [pause 0.4s] It's called the covariance matrix. [pause 0.5s] Once we have it, we never need to touch the points again.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: ch3_s02 -->
What's inside it? [pause 0.4s] Down the diagonal sit the variances we already met: the spread of height, and the spread of arm span. [pause 0.8s] Off the diagonal sits something new, the covariance. [pause 0.4s] For each person, take how far they are from the average height, and multiply it by how far they are from the average arm span. [pause 0.6s] A tall person with long arms gives a positive product. [pause 0.3s] So does a short person with short arms. [pause 0.4s] Mixed cases give negative ones. [pause 0.8s] Average the products. [pause 0.4s] A large positive covariance says the two measurements tend to rise together. [pause 0.6s] And the matrix is symmetric, because height with arm span is the same as arm span with height.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch3_s03 -->
A matrix is also a motion. [pause 0.4s] Apply the covariance matrix to every arrow on a circle, and the circle stretches into an ellipse, tilted along the cloud. [pause 1.0s] And remember the spread we recorded for every angle? [pause 0.4s] Measure how far each stretched arrow reaches along its own original direction. [pause 0.5s] That's the same record, rebuilt from the matrix alone. [pause 1.0s] The matrix knows the variance in every direction.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch3_s04 -->
For the digits, the covariance matrix has sixty-four rows and sixty-four columns, one for each pixel. [pause 0.8s] Each entry says how strongly two pixels brighten together. [pause 0.6s] Neighbouring pixels mostly rise and fall together, because a pen stroke is wider than one square. [pause 0.6s] A few pixels near the edges are blank in every scan, so their rows are empty. [pause 1.0s] Somewhere in this grid of numbers is the best view of the digits.

> [pause 2]

# Eigenvectors

<!-- scene: ch4_s01 -->
Watch what the covariance matrix does to a fan of arrows. [pause 0.8s] Almost every arrow gets stretched and turned off its own line. [pause 0.6s] But two directions only stretch. [pause 0.4s] They stay pointing exactly where they were. [pause 1.0s] Arrows like these are called eigenvectors, from the German word for own. [pause 0.5s] Each one has a number that says how much it's stretched, its eigenvalue. [pause 0.8s] And these two lie right along the long and short axes of our cloud.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch4_s02 -->
Why should the best direction be an eigenvector? [pause 0.5s] Describe any arrow using the two eigenvectors as axes. [pause 0.4s] Its variance becomes a mix of the two eigenvalues, with weights that always add up to one. [pause 1.0s] A mix can never be bigger than its largest ingredient. [pause 0.5s] So the best you can do is put all the weight on the largest eigenvalue. [pause 0.4s] That means pointing straight along its eigenvector. [pause 1.0s] The method of Lagrange multipliers reaches the same place: at the best arrow, the matrix times the arrow points along the arrow itself.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch4_s03 -->
So each eigenvalue has a plain meaning. [pause 0.4s] It's the variance of the data along its eigenvector. [pause 0.8s] And because the covariance matrix is symmetric, its eigenvectors always meet at right angles. [pause 0.6s] That's why the principal components come out perpendicular, with no extra work. [pause 1.0s] Put it together, and the matrix splits into three simple moves: turn to the eigenvector axes, stretch by the eigenvalues, and turn back.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch4_s04 -->
That's the whole method. [pause 0.4s] Centre the data. [pause 0.3s] Build the covariance matrix. [pause 0.3s] Find its eigenvectors. [pause 0.3s] Sort them by eigenvalue, largest first. [pause 0.3s] Then describe every point by its shadows on the top few. [pause 1.2s] No searching, no guessing. [pause 0.4s] The same steps work for two columns, for sixty-four, or for ten thousand.

> [pause 2]

# Cutting Dimensions

<!-- scene: ch5_s01 -->
Back to our people, with three measurements. [pause 0.4s] Their cloud is long, fairly wide, and quite thin, like a pebble. [pause 0.8s] The first two principal components span a flat sheet through the middle of it. [pause 0.6s] Drop every point onto that sheet, and turn the sheet to face us. [pause 1.2s] We've gone from three numbers per person to two. [pause 0.4s] What we threw away is only the short drop from each point to the sheet.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch5_s02 -->
How much did we lose? [pause 0.4s] The eigenvalues answer that. [pause 0.4s] Each one is the variance along its direction, and together they add up to the total variance. [pause 0.8s] So each eigenvalue's share of the total is the share of the variation that direction carries. [pause 1.0s] For the digits, the first two directions carry a little more than a quarter. [pause 0.5s] About twenty of them carry nine tenths. [pause 0.6s] And three carry nothing at all: those are the pixels that are blank in every scan.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch5_s03 -->
Each principal component of the digits is itself a pattern of sixty-four shades, so we can draw it as an image. [pause 0.8s] Every digit is the average digit plus some amount of each pattern. [pause 0.6s] Start from the average, and add the patterns one at a time, largest first. [pause 1.2s] With a few, it's a blur. [pause 0.4s] With ten, you can read it. [pause 0.4s] With twenty, it's hard to tell from the original. [pause 1.0s] So twenty numbers per digit, instead of sixty-four, lose very little.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: ch5_s04 -->
Now the map from the beginning makes sense. [pause 0.4s] Its two axes are the first two principal components. [pause 0.4s] Each dot is one digit, placed by how much of each pattern it contains. [pause 1.0s] Digits that share strokes contain similar amounts, so they land near each other. [pause 1.0s] In practice, nobody builds the covariance matrix for large data. [pause 0.4s] A related factorization, the singular value decomposition, finds the same directions straight from the table, and more accurately. [pause 0.8s] The answer is the same: the directions of greatest spread.

> [pause 2]

# Where PCA Breaks

<!-- scene: ch6_s01 -->
PCA is simple, and that makes its limits easy to see. [pause 0.5s] Suppose we record height in millimetres, but arm span in metres. [pause 0.6s] The height numbers are now a thousand times bigger than the arm span numbers, so their variance is a million times bigger. [pause 0.8s] The first component points almost straight along height, whatever the people are like. [pause 0.8s] The fix is to put every measurement on the same footing first: divide each one by its own spread.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: ch6_s02 -->
PCA also only looks for flat views. [pause 0.4s] Roll a sheet of points into a spiral, like a cinnamon roll. [pause 0.6s] Its best flat shadow squashes the layers on top of each other, and points that were far apart along the sheet land side by side. [pause 0.8s] For curved data like this, people use methods that follow the curve, such as kernel PCA, t-SNE and UMAP.

> [pause 1.2]

<!-- scene: ch6_s03 -->
And the biggest spread is not always the most interesting. [pause 0.4s] Take two groups that are long and thin, lying side by side. [pause 0.6s] Most of the spread runs along their length, so that's where the first component points. [pause 0.6s] Its shadow piles both groups on top of each other. [pause 1.0s] The direction that separates them has very little spread, and PCA ranks it last. [pause 0.8s] PCA finds the view that keeps the most variation. [pause 0.4s] Whether that's the view you need is still your call.

> [pause 2.5]

# Outro

<!-- scene: out_s01 -->
Let's put it all back together. [pause 0.4s] Data becomes a cloud of points. [pause 0.4s] We centre it, and ask which direction spreads the shadows the most. [pause 0.5s] That variance fits inside one symmetric matrix. [pause 0.4s] Its eigenvectors are the answer, and its eigenvalues say how much each one keeps. [pause 0.5s] Keep the top few, and sixty-four numbers become a handful, with most of the picture still there.

> [pause 1.5]

<!-- scene: out_s02 -->
Every view of data throws something away, just like a shadow. [pause 0.6s] PCA doesn't avoid that. [pause 0.3s] It tells you exactly what you kept, and exactly what you lost. [pause 1.0s] So the next time you meet a table with too many columns, turn it to the light first.
